_comment: 🧩️ This subset's own contribution. `s.trinity.rewrite` is a semio-NATIVE graph-rewrite rule whose three authored bodies are opaque JSON strings, so no oracle is registered and the evidence rests on the seven committed per-kind specification vectors plus the inverse law (see noOracleDecisions).

noOracleDecisions.rationale: No third party reads or writes `.rewrite.dsl.semio`, and — the decisive point — no third party could adjudicate this vocabulary even if it did, because the vocabulary deliberately does NOT look inside the thing it edits. `beforeFixtureJson`, `lhsJson` and `rhsJson` are opaque JSON STRINGS on this artifact's wire: a whole `trinity.graph` document, a whole match pattern with its where-clause, and a whole create/delete/set/merge body with its parameter declarations, each replaced atomically by one `edit` verb. A JSON library asked whether `edit-rhs` is correct would be checking that a string parses, which is not the claim. The claim is that a rule is edited body-at-a-time while its two KEY-ADDRESSED maps — `parameterBindings` and `ruleLayout` — are edited key-at-a-time through a `change`/`remove` pair, and that no verb ever reaches across from one to the other. Confidence comes instead from the seven committed, independently handcrafted `(before, mutation, after, diff, outcome)` specification vectors under `../🧬️schema/🧬️mutations/<slug>/🧪️tests/<fixture>/`, each already unit-tested inside the production crate, re-exercised end to end here through `apply_rewrite_mutation_reporting`; and from the inverse law as a metamorphic property, which is the strongest available statement about a `remove` whose undo has to restore a value the payload never carried.
